mcqs.question: In the recursion tree for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, why does every level contribute the same total work (n)?
options: Because the tree only has one level
Because each level has twice as many nodes as the previous but each node does half the work, so the product stays constant
Because n is a fixed constant across all levels
It's a coincidence specific to this recurrence
mcqs.explanation: At depth k there are 2^k subproblems, each of size n/2^k doing n/2^k work, so total work per level is 2^k × (n/2^k) = n — constant across every level, which is exactly why summing log(n) levels of n gives O(n log n).

mcqs.question: Why does Binet's formula F(n) = (φⁿ − ψⁿ)/√5 give an integer even though φ and ψ are irrational?
options: It doesn't — the formula is only an approximation
Because |ψ| < 1, ψⁿ shrinks toward 0, and the irrational parts of φⁿ and ψⁿ cancel exactly, leaving an integer result
Because φ and ψ are actually rational
Because √5 always divides evenly into φⁿ
mcqs.explanation: The formula is exact, not approximate — the irrational components of φⁿ and ψⁿ are constructed (via the characteristic equation roots) to cancel precisely when combined, and since |ψ|<1 its contribution vanishes for large n, but the formula is exact at every n, not just asymptotically.

mcqs.question: You unrolled a recurrence, spotted a clean pattern, and wrote down a closed form. What must you still do before trusting it?
options: Nothing — a clean pattern is proof enough
Verify the closed form against the actual base case(s) and confirm the inductive step
Convert it to a generating function regardless
Re-derive it using the Master theorem instead
mcqs.explanation: Unrolling only produces a candidate formula; without checking it against the real base case and verifying the inductive step, an off-by-one or boundary error can silently slip through — the pattern 'looking clean' isn't itself a proof.
